lessons.title: Getting Started with Java
lessons.summary: Java is a popular programming language used to build applications, websites, mobile software, and many other technologies.

blocks.content: Java is a popular programming language used to build applications, websites, mobile software, and many other technologies.
One of Java’s key strengths is platform independence. A Java program can run on different operating systems with little or no change.
Now it’s time to write your first Java program. Click Next Lesson and begin learning Java with Go Coder.

lessons.title: Course Overview
lessons.summary: This Java course is designed to help you build a strong foundation and gain practical coding skills.

blocks.content: This Java course is designed to help you build a strong foundation and gain practical coding skills.
Here’s how you’ll learn:

blocks.text: 1. Learn Step by Step

blocks.content: Each topic is divided into short lessons, making it easier to understand and follow your progress.

blocks.text: 2. Code and Experiment

blocks.content: After learning a concept, use the code editor to write, run, and modify programs. Practice is the key to improving your coding skills.

blocks.text: 3. Practice What You Learn

blocks.content: Solve coding exercises after each topic to check your understanding and improve your problem-solving ability.
By the end of the course, you’ll have written many Java programs and built practical projects that prepare you for real-world development.

lessons.title: Introduction to Data Types
lessons.summary: Programs work with different kinds of information. Java uses data types to identify what kind of value a program is handling.

blocks.content: Programs work with different kinds of information. Java uses data types to identify what kind of value a program is handling.
In this lesson, you’ll explore:

- Numbers
- Text
- Characters

blocks.text: Let’s begin with Numbers.

lessons.summary: Java mainly works with two types of numeric values:

blocks.content: Java mainly works with two types of numeric values:

blocks.text: 1. Integers

blocks.content: Integers are whole numbers without decimal points. They can be positive, negative, or zero.
Examples: 8, -4, 0, 25

blocks.text: 2. Decimal Numbers

blocks.content: Decimal numbers contain a fractional part. They can also be positive, negative, or zero.

blocks.text: In Java, we commonly use the double type to store decimal values.

lessons.title: Introduction to Variables
lessons.summary: So far, you’ve learned how to work with numbers, text, and characters in Java.

blocks.content: So far, you’ve learned how to work with numbers, text, and characters in Java.

blocks.text: But programs often need to store values and use them again. This is where variables are useful.

blocks.content: A variable is a named storage location that holds a value.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to:

- Create variables
- Store values in variables
- Display variable values
Let’s begin by creating a variable.

lessons.title: Creating Variables
lessons.summary: For example:

blocks.text: A variable is created by specifying its data type followed by its name.

blocks.content: For example:
int score;
Here:

- score is the variable name.
- int tells Java that the variable stores an integer.
Figure: Creating a Variable
At this stage, score has no value. Next, let’s learn how to assign a value to it.

lessons.title: Assigning Values to Variables
lessons.summary: After creating a variable, we can store a value in it using the = operator.

blocks.content: After creating a variable, we can store a value in it using the = operator.
int score;
score = 50;
Here, 50 is assigned to the variable score.
Figure: Assigning a Value to a Variable

lessons.title: Declaring and Assigning a Value Together
lessons.summary: int score = 50;

blocks.text: Java allows you to create a variable and give it a value in the same statement.

blocks.content: int score = 50;
Here, score is declared as an integer and immediately assigned the value 50.
This is the same as writing:
int score;
score = 50;
Using one statement is a shorter way to declare and initialize a variable.
Next, let’s practice identifying variables in Java.

lessons.title: Understanding Variables and Data Types
lessons.summary: For example:

blocks.text: A variable stores a value, while a data type tells Java what kind of value can be stored.

blocks.content: For example:
int score = 88;
Here, int is the data type and score is the variable. Since int is used, score can hold whole numbers.
Java offers several data types for working with numbers, characters, text, and other values. Let’s explore them one by one.

lessons.title: Common Java Data Types
lessons.summary: Java provides different data types for storing different kinds of values. In this lesson, we’ll focus on three commonly used types:

blocks.content: Java provides different data types for storing different kinds of values. In this lesson, we’ll focus on three commonly used types:

blocks.text: 1. int – Stores whole numbers without decimal points, such as 25, -8, and 100.
2. double – Stores numbers that contain decimal values, such as 12.5 and -4.75.
3. char – Stores a single character, such as 'A', '7', or '#'.

blocks.content: You’ve already seen int variables. Next, we’ll learn how to work with double and char values.

lessons.title: Creating Double and Char Variables
lessons.summary: Java uses different data types for different kinds of values.

blocks.content: Java uses different data types for different kinds of values.
For decimal numbers, we can use double:
double price = 1499.75;
For a single character, we can use char:
char grade = 'A';
The double value can contain decimals, while char stores one character inside single quotes.
Next, let’s learn how to display a double value.

lessons.summary: Variables become useful when a program needs to work with values that may change.

blocks.content: Variables become useful when a program needs to work with values that may change.

For example, a student's score may change as they complete more activities. Let’s see how Java allows us to update a variable.

blocks.content: When changing a variable's value, we don't write the data type again. We simply use the variable name with the assignment operator (=).

blocks.content: A variable can hold a new value of the same compatible data type.

lessons.title: Choosing Good Variable Names
lessons.summary: A good variable name makes your code easier to read and understand.

blocks.content: A good variable name makes your code easier to read and understand.
Compare these examples:
double p = 2499.50;
and
double productPrice = 2499.50;
Figure: Good and Bad Variable Names
productPrice is a better choice because its name clearly describes the value it stores.

blocks.text: Rules for Naming Variables

blocks.content:
- Use meaningful names
Choose a name that describes the stored value.
- Use camelCase for multiple words
Start the first word with lowercase and capitalize the beginning of each following word.

blocks.code:
int studentMarks = 85;
double totalPrice = 450.75;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: Figure: Good and Bad Variable Names

blocks.text: Invalid Variable Names

blocks.content: Java does not allow spaces or most special symbols in variable names. A variable name also cannot begin with a number.

blocks.code:
int student marks = 90; // Invalid
int 2marks = 90; // Invalid
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: Java also has reserved keywords that cannot be used as variable names, such as int, double, and char.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.content: Choose variable names that tell the reader what the value represents.

blocks.text: 3. Case Sensitivity

lessons.title: Introduction to Data Conversion

lessons.title: Automatic Type Conversion

lessons.title: Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming
lessons.summary: Java is designed around Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), a programming approach that helps organize code into reusable and manageable parts.

blocks.content: Java is designed around Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), a programming approach that helps organize code into reusable and manageable parts.
The two basic building blocks of OOP are:

- Classes
- Objects
These concepts may seem unfamiliar at first, but we'll learn them step by step using simple examples.

blocks.text: Let’s begin by understanding what a class is.

lessons.title: Classes in OOP
lessons.summary: You’ve already been using classes in your programs. For example:

blocks.text: A class is a blueprint that groups related code and describes what a Java program can contain.

blocks.content: You’ve already been using classes in your programs. For example:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: Here, class Main creates a class named Main. The statements inside its braces belong to that class.

blocks.text: Think of a class as a design or blueprint that can be used to organize related data and behavior.
As you continue learning OOP, you’ll see how classes work together with objects.
Next, let’s understand what an object is.

lessons.title: Objects in OOP
lessons.summary: An object is an instance created from a class. While a class provides the design, an object lets us work with that design in a program.

blocks.content: An object is an instance created from a class. While a class provides the design, an object lets us work with that design in a program.
To create an object of the Main class, we can write:

blocks.code: Main program = new Main();
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Figure: Syntax to Create an Object

blocks.content: Here:

- new Main() creates a new object from the Main class.
- program stores a reference to that object.
- Main is the data type of the program variable because the object belongs to the Main class.

blocks.text: You can think of a class as a blueprint and an object as something created using that blueprint.

blocks.content: For now, we'll keep our examples simple and gradually learn how objects can be used with custom classes and methods.

lessons.title: OOP in Java
lessons.summary: Classes and objects are important parts of Java, and they will become easier to understand as you practice more.

blocks.content: Classes and objects are important parts of Java, and they will become easier to understand as you practice more.
For now, keep these two ideas in mind:

- Classes organize the structure and behavior of a Java program.
- Objects are created from classes and allow us to work with their features.

blocks.text: We'll explore OOP concepts in greater detail in Chapter 4.

blocks.content: Next, we'll learn how to make Java programs more interactive by accepting input from the user. This will help us build programs that can work with information provided at runtime.

lessons.title: Introduction to User Input
lessons.summary: So far, our programs have used values that we entered directly into the code.

blocks.content: So far, our programs have used values that we entered directly into the code.
For exam

blocks.code: int score = 50;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: But real programs often need to receive information from the person using them.

blocks.text: Java allows us to take input from the user and use that information while the program is running.

blocks.content: Next, we'll learn how to accept user input and use it in our programs.

lessons.title: Taking User Input
lessons.summary: There are four main steps involved:

blocks.text: Java provides the Scanner class to read information entered by the user.

blocks.content: There are four main steps involved:

- Import Scanner – Make the class available in your program.
- Create a Scanner object – Set up an object that can read input.
- Read user input – Use the Scanner object to receive data.
- Close the Scanner – Close it when input is no longer needed.
We'll explore each step with simple examples in the upcoming lessons.

lessons.summary: After finishing the input process, we can close the Scanner object using:

lessons.title: Input Prompts
lessons.summary: A prompt is a message shown to the user before the program waits for input. It isn't required for Scanner to work, but it helps users understand what they should enter.

blocks.content: A prompt is a message shown to the user before the program waits for input. It isn't required for Scanner to work, but it helps users understand what they should enter.
For example, without a prompt:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: The program waits for input, but the user isn't told what to enter.
A better approach is to display a clear prompt:

blocks.code:
System.out.println("Enter your marks:");
int marks = reader.nextInt();
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: Now the user immediately knows what information the program expects.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.content: Prompts aren't required, but they make interactive programs easier to understand and use.

lessons.title: Swapping Two Variables
lessons.summary: Sometimes we need to exchange the values stored in two variables.

blocks.content: Sometimes we need to exchange the values stored in two variables.
Suppose we have:

blocks.code:
int firstValue = 15;
int secondValue = 30;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: After swapping, we want:

blocks.code:
firstValue = 30
secondValue = 15
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: Before learning the correct method, let's look at an approach that doesn't work:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.code:
First Value: 30
Second Value: 30
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.content: The values were not swapped correctly. When firstValue = secondValue runs, the original value of firstValue is lost.
Can you figure out how we can preserve the original value before making the exchange?

lessons.title: Problem with the Code
lessons.summary: Figure: Initial Values of the Variables

blocks.text: At the beginning, firstValue contains 15, while secondValue contains 30.

blocks.content: Figure: Initial Values of the Variables
When this statement runs:

blocks.code: firstValue = secondValue;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: firstValue becomes 30. The original value 15 is no longer available in firstValue.
Now both variables contain 30:

blocks.code:
firstValue = 30
secondValue = 30
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: Figure: Update The Values
When we then execute:

blocks.code: secondValue = firstValue;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: we simply assign 30 to secondValue again. The original value 15 cannot be recovered.

blocks.content: This is why the swapping attempt fails.
Figure: Final Values
To swap the values correctly, we need a way to temporarily store one value before replacing it. We'll explore that approach next.

lessons.title: Swapping Two Variables
lessons.summary: To swap two values without losing either one, we can use a temporary variable. The temporary variable holds the first value while the other values are rearranged.

blocks.content: To swap two values without losing either one, we can use a temporary variable. The temporary variable holds the first value while the other values are rearranged.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.code:
First Value: 30
Second Value: 15
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: How It Works

blocks.content: The swap happens in three steps:

- temp saves the original value of firstValue (15).
- firstValue receives the value of secondValue (30).
- secondValue receives the saved value from temp (15).
So the values are successfully exchanged without losing the original value.

blocks.text: What You’ve Covered

blocks.content:
- Variables and Data Types — Store different kinds of information in Java.
- Output Statements — Display values and messages using System.out.println().
- Arithmetic Operators — Perform calculations using +, -, *, /, and %.
- Increment and Decrement — Modify values using ++ and --.
- Type Conversion — Convert values between compatible data types.
- Classes and Objects — Understand the basic foundation of OOP in Java.
- User Input — Accept integer and decimal values using Scanner.
- Multiple Inputs — Read and process more than one value.
- Practical Programs — Apply these concepts to conversions, calculations, discounts, and variable swapping.
You now have the foundation needed to understand more advanced Java concepts.
